item.title: I Designed a Custom Robot Controller PCB from Scratch
item.content:encoded:
Then 419 DRC Errors Told Me I Was Wrong

From a dead robot and two abandoned power architectures to a PCBWay-manufactured controller that survived its first physical inspection.

In an earlier robotics article, I placed two robots next to each other and described one of them as the more advanced platform I intended to develop next.

This project is the follow-through on that promise — but not in the neat, linear way that sentence might suggest.

The starting point was a non-functioning two-wheel robot with an undocumented controller, an extremely discharged battery and very little trustworthy design information. The endpoint documented here is a manufactured, unpopulated controller carrier PCB that passed a selected set of incoming continuity and isolation checks and was accepted for controlled assembly.

That distinction matters.

This is not yet the story of a finished autonomous robot. It is the engineering record of how I moved from assumptions to evidence: opening the chassis, measuring what was actually there, defining requirements, rejecting two architectures, building the schematic in KiCad, checking footprints against real parts, comparing ten routed layouts, undoing a repair that produced 419 design-rule violations, auditing the manufacturing outputs and inspecting the boards after delivery.

PCBWay sponsored the manufacture of the bare PCBs. The design decisions, mistakes, verification limits and conclusions in this article remain my own. Sponsorship made the manufacturing milestone possible; it did not certify the electrical design or require a positive verdict.

The robot I opened was not the robot I had imagined

My initial mental model was close to a bare educational chassis: two motors, a battery and enough free space to install a new controller. Removing the upper deck immediately changed that model.

Inside was a RoboPad RP-B0027 board, an SN754410NE motor driver, two geared motors, an enclosed battery and several wires whose functions had not been established.

A loose three wire connection was initially treated as an unused accessory. Further inspection showed red, blue and black conductors entering the LiPo pouch, making a two-cell balance connection a much more plausible interpretation.

This was the first useful correction: the visible destination of a loose connector was not enough to identify it. I needed to trace the leads and define what I was measuring.

The original controller also failed to respond during an attempted battery powered test. It would have been tempting to write that the controller was broken.

I cannot support that conclusion.

The battery was later shown to be severely discharged, so the test did not isolate the controller as the fault. So, I removed the RoboPad because I wanted a documented, programmable control path — not because I had proved that its IC had failed.

Measurement only helps when the boundary is clear

The first voltage investigation mixed two different measurement points: the isolated battery output and robot-side wiring downstream of connectors and switches. A negative display can simply indicate reversed probe polarity; the more important question is what node the probes are touching.

The measurement sequence moved from robot-side wiring to the battery side output. The old 2S pack produced a reading around half a volt, while a separate cell showed 3.47 V as a plausibility check.

So the useful observations were:

• An early robot side discussion centred on approximately -0.41V, but the measurement boundary was not yet isolated.

• On 28 July, I explicitly measured 0.41 V at the battery-side red and black leads.

• A later photograph showed a reading interpreted as approximately 0.55 V. The image does not justify inventing more precision than that.

• A separate comparison cell displayed 3.47 V, which helped show that the meter and contact method were capable of producing a plausible cell reading.

The old pack label stated 2S, 7.4 V nominal, 1,000 mAh and 7.4 Wh. Those printed ratings described the product, not the present condition of this particular pack. The terminal measurements were the stronger evidence. I stopped treating the old LiPo as a usable supply and moved the design basis to a six-cell, 7.2 V NiMH system.

I also considered an RS PRO 7.2 V, 1.3 Ah NiMH pack that I already owned. One terminal remained enclosed by plastic, so I never obtained a valid voltage or capacity result from the available evidence. “Already owned” and “labelled correctly” did not make it verified hardware.

The chassis dimensions had to become electrical constraints

The next missing step was mechanical. A schematic can look convincing while having no credible path into the robot.

Ruler photographs and a local deck annotation established the approximate envelope. The roughly 8 x 6.5 cm marked area was one local region, not the complete chassis size.

The outer platform was approximately 155 x 115 mm.

Depending on whether the existing holder remained, it was safest to constrain the usable length to around 60 mm or 100 mm, with about 100 mm of usable width.

The available height was around 20 mm and the plywood was approximately 5 mm thick.

Other local constraints included an 85 x 40 mm battery case, a switch opening around 15 mm and a wheel gap of only about 2 mm.

Several numbers needed interpretation rather than automatic entry into CAD. A reported “70 mm standoff,” for example, referred to overall height rather than a mounting-post spacing. A “155 mm between wheels” description was not a verified track width.

The useful lesson was that every dimension needed a named physical meaning.

I eventually froze the carrier PCB at 95 x 55 mm with four M3 mounting holes. And so the proposed hole centres, relative to the board origin, were (5, 5), (90, 5), (5, 50) and (90, 50) mm — these were approved new drilling positions, not measurements of existing holes.

Lastly, a print to scale template of the dimensions was produced, but I do not have a photographed completed fit check, so the populated-board and harness clearances remain an assembly-stage requirement.

I defined success before choosing the final controller

“Make the robot drive straight” is too vague to design or test against.

I converted that ambition into a preliminary acceptance target: travel 3 m on a laminate floor and finish within 100 mm of the intended endpoint, repeated across five runs. I also wanted an obstacle response that stopped the robot and waited.

A 100 mm lateral offset over 3 m corresponds to an idealised constant heading error of about 1.91 degrees. That calculation is only a way to understand the tolerance.

It is not a measured accuracy claim.

Wheel-diameter mismatch, slip, starting alignment, encoder calibration and controller behaviour all still matter.

The controller decision also needed to include the hardware I already had.

The owned ATmega328P Nano and the original motor were genuine candidates; so I ran a basic blink test that verified programming and LED operation, but not motor drive or wireless control.

I ran Blink on my existing ATmega328P-based Nano and changed the delay to confirm that I could program it and observe the expected behaviour. Reusing it would have reduced immediate cost and it remained useful for experiments. However, it did not provide the integrated wireless path I wanted for laptop/phone control and/or future expansion.

As a result, I chose the Nano ESP32 as the primary selected controller. Its Nano form factor did not make it electrically interchangeable with the classic 5 V Nano: the logic system is 3.3 V and every interface had to be checked on that basis.

The original Nano was not “rejected because it was old.” It was retained as a valid bench tool while the Nano ESP32 better matched the project requirements.

The first custom board tried to do too much

My first architecture attempted to integrate the controller, motor driver, power conversion, current sensing, protection and sensor interfaces on one PCB.

In principle, that would have produced a compact and very impressive board.

In practice, however, it concentrated too many unverified assumptions into the first fabrication.

The branch considered DRV8833 and later DRV8411 motor-driver directions, separate TPS54302 and AP63205 conversion stages and a removable classic Nano.

It did not fail on physical hardware because it was never fabricated.

It failed a pre-build design review.

The problems were not cosmetic:

• The proposed DRV8833 current-limit explanation referred to an IPROPI arrangement that the device does not use. Its current-sense implementation is based on AISEN and BISEN.

• Regulator models contained invented output connections, bootstrap capacitors returned to ground, a missing feedback path and input capacitors that were not actually connected into a complete circuit.

• Nano and peripheral return paths were missing, one controller pin appeared on conflicting nets and an LED connection was incomplete.

• A unidirectional TVS was reversed, meaning a protection component could have created the fault it was intended to prevent.

• A 2920 resettable fuse had been assigned an 1812 footprint, an SMBJ device had an SMA footprint, female Nano sockets were represented by unsuitable SMD male headers and a terminal-block pitch did not match the intended part.

• A presentation PNG and a manually assembled netlist were being treated as if they were authoritative editable design sources.

This is why showing the abandoned branch matters. Without it, the final modular board appears to have been an obvious first choice.

As a result, I abandoned the integrated architecture because the modelling, package control and validation burden were too high for the evidence I had.

The second architecture reduced the number of simultaneous unknowns

The revised design separated the high current motor path from the custom PCB.

A Cytron MDD3A module would handle the motor switching, while the 95 x 55 mm carrier would provide the Nano ESP32 sockets, protected logic input, battery monitoring, motor-driver logic connections, encoder conditioning and expansion interfaces.

The modular architecture. Encoder and expansion signals terminate on the carrier; high-current motor power remains external through the MDD3A.

That distinction prevents an important misunderstanding: the carrier fuse and copper do not protect or carry the motor current.

The MDD3A auxiliary output was treated in the design conversations as a 5 V, 200 mA source for relevant low power functions, whereas the main battery-to-driver-to-motor path remained separate.

Modularity did not make verification optional.

It simply made the first controlled bring-up more tractable.

If the carrier, motor power stage, encoder electronics and firmware all changed at the same time, a failure would be harder to localise.

The power input and battery monitor were small circuits with important details

The carrier input included a 1.1 A hold resettable fuse, an AO3407A P-channel MOSFET for reverse-polarity protection and a divider/filter for monitoring the protected supply.

The preserved RC2 connectivity. Q1 pad 3 is the BAT_FUSED drain, pad 2 is the NANO_VIN source and pad 1 is the gate. The ADC divider measures the protected NANO_VIN node, not the raw battery terminals independently.

The divider uses 47kOhm over 15kOhm, followed by a 1 kOhm series resistor and 100nF capacitor at the ADC node. Its ideal ratio is:

15 / (47 + 15) = 0.24194

At 7.2 V on NANO_VIN, the ideal ADC voltage is about 1.742 V. At an assumed 8.7 V, it is approximately 2.105 V. The divider current at 7.2 V is only around 116 microamps.

That calculation later mattered because an automated layout assumption incorrectly treated the divider net as a 500 mA power path.

The ADC sees an approximate source resistance of 47 kOhm in parallel with 15 kOhm, plus the 1 kOhm series resistor: about 12.37 kOhm.

And with the 100nF capacitor, the simple small signal time constant is approximately 1.237 ms.

These are design calculations, not measurements. Whereas, ADC calibration, component tolerance, DC-bias capacitance and sampling behaviour remain bench questions.

Pin mapping was part of the circuit, not an afterthought

The motor logic was assigned to D2-D5. The four conditioned encoder channels used D6-D9. A0 measured the protected supply. The user button moved to A6/GPIO13 after the earlier A2/GPIO3 assignment raised a strap-sensitive pin concern. A4 and A5 were reserved for I2C, while D10-D13 formed the SPI expansion group.

The six-pin MDD3A logic harness was frozen as:

1. MDD 5 V auxiliary

2. Ground

3. Motor 1A

4. Motor 1B

5. Motor 2A

6. Motor 2B

Wire colour can make assembly easier, but colour is not pin identity. Each real cable still needs a continuity map before connection.

The encoder-supply selector also needed explicit behaviour. JP1 selects either 3.3 V or the MDD3A auxiliary rail onto ENC_VCC. It must never short the two source rails together. J3 and J4 carry supply, ground and raw A/B channels from the left and right encoders.

One of four encoder channels: the 1 kOhm and 1nF input network feeds an SN74LVC14A Schmitt-trigger inverter powered from 3.3 V; the optional pull-up is DNP until the encoder output type is known.

Each 1kOhm/1nF network has a nominal time constant of 1 microsecond and a simple pole near 159kHz. The Schmitt-trigger input adds hysteresis, but the output is inverted, so firmware must use a consistent direction and count convention. More importantly, filtering and hysteresis are provisions — not proof that motor noise has been eliminated. I still need encoder waveforms, supply verification, counts per wheel revolution and calibration data.

The sensor interface also changed during development. An early HC-SR04 proposal would have required Echo-level adaptation. The final carrier instead exposes a 3.3 V Grove-style ultrasonic interface. Treating those two interfaces as the same circuit would hide a real design change.

The missing middle was the native KiCad schematic

Earlier summaries jumped from controller analysis to PCB layout as though the board emerged directly from a block diagram. The middle work was where many of the most useful failures occurred.

The first generated schematic produced 5 errors and 146 warnings. Fixing it was not a single clean pass:

• A manual review had the AO3407A source and drain exchanged.

• A generated file contained invalid hidden-property syntax near line 1282 and would not parse correctly.

• Intermediate repairs produced 9 errors and 5 warnings, then 6 errors and 6 warnings.

• Nano net-to-pin and UUID associations were still wrong, so incremental editing was no longer trustworthy.

• I rebuilt the representation from the legacy source, recording 66 symbol instances, 186 pins and 46 named nets.

• A user-run ERC after conversion reported 0 errors and 0 warnings, with four ignored test categories reviewed separately.

Even that last result needs qualification.

The preserved schematic models module and IC pins as passive, which weakens ERC’s ability to detect functional input, output and power conflicts.

Zero reported ERC issues therefore meant that a particular configured rule gate passed. However, it did not prove that every device function, pin mapping or footprint was correct.

When the PCB first opened, native DRC reported 347 items. Among them were 138 expected unconnected items before routing, 25 shorts, 9 clearance violations, 25 solder-mask bridges and 2 hole-to-hole violations, plus other categories. Overlapping placement and malformed U2 geometry were real physical problems. Electrical connectivity alone had not made the board manufacturable.

Footprints turned part numbers into physical commitments

A symbol says what a component does. A footprint decides whether the component can be soldered to the board at all.

Native geometry checks for the Nano sockets, SOIC-14 logic IC, AO3407A, tactile switch, Grove connector and JST-SH connector. Pitch, pad numbering, drill and retention features all mattered.

The footprint review changed several decisions:

• The first turned pin Nano socket option had a mating range poorly suited to the Nano’s approximately 0.64 mm square posts. So, I selected two Harwin CN25444 1 x 15 socket rows instead.

• SN74LVC14AD stock was limited, whereas the SN74LVC14ADR was available. The R suffix changed the packaging format, not the SOIC “D” land pattern. Other suffixes such as DBR or PWR would imply different packages.

• A generic four-leg 6 mm tactile switch did not match the board’s two-contact pattern. And so a TS31S, with 6.5 mm contact spacing, became the selected part.

• The Grove connector used 2 mm pitch, not the common 2.54 mm header pitch.

• The JST-SH footprint remained unresolved because the preserved board contained four signal pads but no separate metal anchor pads.

That last point is still open.

Earlier purchasing guidance correctly advised against ordering the JST-SH connector until the footprint was resolved. A later basket included the part without showing a corrected PCB. The shopping decision did not overrule the native geometry. Before population, the received connector, manufacturer drawing and board must be compared and the result recorded as populate, DNP or rework.

Placement came before routing — and failed in several different ways

Placement had to respect the Nano antenna, connector access, battery entry, mounting holes, decoupling distances and the limited chassis envelope.

One handoff was described as nearly routed, but inspection showed zero tracks, zero vias and zero copper zones. A later custom-routing attempt contained roughly 1,110 segments and 32 vias but still had four unresolved connections. Another checkpoint recorded 1,225 segments, 75 vias and a custom connectivity pass across 45 non-ground nets. These were useful intermediate states, but none was equivalent to a native KiCad release.

I then moved the board into the Quilter workflow. The first nested archive did not import as intended. Supplying the native project files allowed the 95 x 55 mm design to be parsed. The routing constraints were recorded as 0.254 mm track width, 0.152 mm clearance, 0.61 mm via diameter, 0.305 mm drill and 0.508 mm edge margin.

The optimiser assumptions also needed correction:

• Both copper layers were signal layers; there was no dedicated uninterrupted ground plane.

• An antenna shape on a drawing layer did not enforce a copper exclusion, so actual keepout areas had to be added.

• Fixing all 70 imported objects prevented poor bypass placement from improving, so 41 components were released while 29 mechanically important objects remained fixed.

• BAT_DIV was wrongly classified as a 500 mA net even though the divider current was in microamps.

• Signal-filter capacitors C3 and C6-C9 were incorrectly identified as bypass capacitors; those false associations were removed while nine genuine bypass assignments were retained.

The approximately 0.267 mm trace-width result for some 1 A assumptions came from a thermal model. It was not a measured temperature rise or proof of transient performance.

Ten candidates existed, and most were not failures

Candidate 10 is the design that appears in the final project images, but it was not the only candidate. Omitting the other nine made the selection look arbitrary and erased the actual decision process.

The provisional ranking after excluding the problem candidates was 10, 8, 4, 6, 5, 3, 2. Candidates 2, 3, 5 and 6 were ranked lower without a documented electrical defect or a quantitative benchmark of route length, via count or performance. Inventing faults for them now would make the story cleaner but less true.

Candidate 10 used a more distributed route pattern, while Candidate 8 showed a more concentrated lower-layer bundle. This was a qualitative ground-copper and congestion judgement, not a measured EMI result.

Candidate 10 was favoured because the displayed routing, seven power-net checks and nine bypass checks passed, the antenna and mounting keepouts appeared clear, U2 sat sensibly between the encoder inputs and Nano, and the encoder-filter components were grouped around that logic. Candidate 8’s bottom-layer bundle appeared more disruptive to a future ground pour.

Candidate 10 still used substantial bottom-layer signal routing. I cannot claim that it was mathematically optimal, lower-noise in operation or electrically superior based on those images alone.

There was also a traceability failure after the decision: a later upload contained Candidate 8 even though Candidate 10 had been selected. The mismatch was caught before release changes. A decision written in a conversation is not enough if the next archive contains a different source file.

The 419 error repair was more important than the attractive layout

The most dramatic failure came after Candidate 10 had been selected. A confident explanation proposed that the imported board used the wrong rotation convention and that nested footprint pads should be transformed. I accepted the repair path before native verification had justified it.

KiCad DRC returned 419 violations and 42 unconnected items.

The native verification sequence. The 419-violation state was rejected and rolled back; the final historical release retained 46 explicit library-footprint mismatch warnings.

The correct response was not to keep patching the transformed file. I restored the original Candidate 10 geometry and treated the native tool as the authority:

This was not a zero-warning board. The 46 mismatches recorded differences between embedded board footprints and library versions. They remained in the release record instead of being hidden.

Some cleanup also had secondary consequences. Moving connector and test-point geometry required care because plated junctions could connect on both copper layers. Removing conflicting silkscreen improved manufacturability, but references R6-R9 later became harder to locate during probing. A visual improvement created a documentation cost.

The title of this article says the errors told me I was wrong.

However, more precisely, they showed that a plausible geometric explanation and a confident repair were not substitutes for opening the native design and running the native checks.

Manufacturing files needed their own audit

A correct board source can still be handed to a manufacturer incorrectly. Gerber and drill output therefore became a separate verification gate.

Top and bottom manufacturing-layer views. These are not assembled-board photographs; they are checks of what the fabricator would receive.

Imported layer labels had to be mapped to the intended top and bottom copper, mask and silkscreen files. An empty bottom-silkscreen file was excluded. Misleading controlled-impedance metadata was removed because controlled impedance had not been designed or specified. Plated and non-plated drill outputs were separated.

The order was for five bare boards: 95 x 55 mm, two-layer FR-4 TG150, 1.6 mm thick, 1 oz copper, green solder mask, white silkscreen and HASL with lead. Those are historical build settings, not proof that the board had been assembled, powered or validated in a robot.

A delivered PCB was a new object that needed new evidence

The boards arrived in August 2026. Arrival was a meaningful milestone, but it did not convert the design calculations into measured performance.

I observed a film or residue on the board. Several explanations were possible, but I had no laboratory identification.

I removed the residue using isopropyl alcohol. The defensible conclusion is narrow: the film was removable, but its origin remains unconfirmed. It would be wrong to turn that observation into proof of solder-mask failure, chemical damage or a defective manufacturing batch.

The incoming inspection was deliberately unpowered. Empty resistor, fuse and IC footprints interrupt paths by design, so an open reading can be correct. Conversely, a continuity beep confirms a selected conductive path under the meter’s threshold; it is not a calibrated low-resistance measurement and says nothing about current capacity.

The report recorded 32 selected checks covering ground distribution, supply-to-ground isolation, the input-protection path, encoder-supply selection, A/B channel isolation and a sample of plated through-holes.

Five representative front-to-back hole checks passed. The M3 mounting holes were correctly treated as non-plated.

The board was accepted for controlled assembly.

That does not mean that every pad was tested, that every net had a resistance value, or that the populated circuit works.

One apparent failure demonstrated why probe instructions also need verification.

I was told to expect continuity from the fuse output to the wrong Q1 pad.

My repeated observations did not match the instruction. Checking the source showed the released mapping:

• Q1 pad 3: drain and BAT_FUSED

• Q1 pad 2: source and NANO_VIN

• Q1 pad 1: gate

The board’s behaviour was consistent with its source once the mapping was corrected. The failure was in the interpretation and documentation; this did not demonstrate defective copper.

Procurement was another verification layer

The later purchasing work exposed problems that a schematic-only review could not:

• A connector can have the correct pitch but the wrong mating contact range.

• Stock substitutions are only safe when the package and electrical function remain compatible.

• A generic tactile switch can look right while its contact geometry is wrong.

• Five spare PCBs do not automatically imply parts for five complete robots.

• DNP components must be separated from genuinely missing parts.

• Main motor wiring and low-current signal wiring are different harness classes; the external main path moved from an 18 AWG proposal to 16 AWG.

There is also an unresolved capacitor specification discrepancy. An earlier requirement called for 10 microfarad, 25V, 0805 X7R parts at C1 and C4. A later selected Murata part was identified as X5R, and a subsequent BOM approval did not record the dielectric exception. That does not prove the X5R capacitor will fail. It means nominal capacitance and voltage are not the entire comparison; the received part number, operating temperature and effective capacitance under DC bias still need a deliberate disposition.

The soldering workstation evolved in the same evidence-driven way. Right-handed working position, short equipment leads and existing inventory changed the layout. A supposedly missing ESD connection turned out to be removable crocodile adapters over 4 mm banana plugs. That mechanical discovery avoided another purchase, but it did not certify the resistance or performance of the ESD setup. Those measurements were proposed and remain to be recorded.

What exists now — and what does not

As documented through 13 September 2026, the project has:

• A defined modular Rev A architecture using a Nano ESP32 carrier and external MDD3A motor stage.

• A 95 x 55 mm native KiCad design with documented pin maps, protection, monitoring, encoder conditioning and expansion interfaces.

• Ten preserved routing candidates with honest dispositions rather than a single unexplained winner.

• Candidate 10 restored after the failed transformation and carried through RC2 with 0 unconnected items, no remaining reported geometric errors and 46 retained footprint-library warnings.

• A reviewed Gerber and drill package and five manufactured bare PCBs.

• Photographic inspection and 32 selected unpowered continuity or isolation checks, including correction of the Q1 false alarm.

• Parts procurement and assembly preparation with J6 and C1/C4 exceptions still open.

It does not yet have evidence for:

• A populated carrier operating from a current-limited supply.

• Verified 3.3 V, 5 V auxiliary or NANO_VIN behaviour under load.

• A proven reverse-polarity event, battery ADC calibration or thermal margin.

• Captured encoder waveforms, calibrated counts per revolution or confirmed noise immunity.

• A complete laptop command path and loss-of-link behaviour.

• Five 3 m driving results, including failed runs, or the obstacle stop-and-wait result.

The next stage is therefore controlled assembly, not a victory lap.

I need to close the J6 and capacitor decisions, document the mechanical fit, inspect each populated stage, establish the power rails before fitting the Nano, verify logic and encoder interfaces, and only then integrate the motor stage. Motion testing follows those gates.

What this project changed about how I engineer as a student

The most valuable output is not Candidate 10 by itself. It is the habit of preserving the chain from assumption to evidence.

Opening the robot replaced a guessed chassis with actual hardware. Defining the probe location changed an ambiguous voltage into a useful battery diagnosis. Measuring the deck turned a PCB outline into a mechanical commitment. Testing the owned Nano kept a genuine alternative in the decision. Rejecting the integrated board prevented plausible-looking circuit errors from becoming copper. Native KiCad checks exposed problems that screenshots and structural parsers could not. Footprint review connected part numbers to physical mating. Ten routing candidates revealed where a preference was qualitative rather than a failure. The 419-error repair proved that confident automation still needs an authoritative verification loop. Incoming inspection then showed that even a delivered board can generate false alarms when documentation points to the wrong pad.

For the next article, I want the evidence to include every powered stage and every motion trial — not only the successful ones. The finished story should show the same things this design stage taught me: what I expected, what I measured, why they differed, what I changed and whether the retest actually closed the issue.

That is a slower way to tell a robotics story. It is also a much more honest way to engineer one.

Technical evidence basis

This article was reconstructed from the project’s Rev B engineering record, native KiCad schematic and PCB sources, routing-candidate archive, manufacturing outputs, procurement discussions, incoming-inspection report and dated photographs. Component behaviour was checked against the relevant Arduino Nano ESP32, TI SN74LVC14A, AO3407A and connector documentation used during the project. Calculated values are identified as calculations; unpowered checks are not presented as powered performance.

PCBWay sponsorship and initial manufacturing feedback

PCBWay sponsored the manufacture of five bare PCBs for this project, allowing the design to progress from digital verification to physical inspection and preparation for assembly.

I would also like to thank Emily Li from PCBWay’s Marketing Department for coordinating the sponsorship and remaining in contact while the article developed into a more complete engineering record. Communication was clear and patient, particularly as documenting the rejected designs and verification work took longer than originally expected.

The incoming inspection included 32 selected unpowered continuity and isolation checks on the inspected board, including checks of ground distribution, the input-protection path, supply selection, encoder signals and representative plated through-holes. The inspected board was accepted for controlled assembly.

This remains initial feedback. The PCB has not yet been populated or powered, so I cannot currently assess operation under load, thermal performance or behaviour inside the robot. I intend to update the project after assembly and controlled bring-up.

PCBWay did not determine the design decisions, testing methods or technical conclusions presented in this article. The failures, unresolved questions and verification limits have been retained because they form part of the engineering record.

item.title: The Pull Request Is Becoming an Evidence Package
item.content:encoded:
In the AI era, a pull request should no longer ask a human to inspect a diff. It should present the evidence needed to make a decision.

A developer can now generate in minutes what previously took hours. Refactoring, test creation, and repetitive implementation work happen at a speed human teams have never operated at before.

Yet most engineering organizations still route these changes through the same pull-request process they used a few years ago.

That creates a problem.

A three-line authorization change can be more dangerous than a 500-line UI refactor. A tiny event-schema change can affect five services, while a large documentation change affects none.

The question is no longer simply:

How do we review more code?

It is:

What evidence do we need before this change deserves to move forward, and who needs to make the remaining decision?

The diff tells us what changed. It does not necessarily tell us what the change can affect, what must be true for it to be safe, or how much human judgment it deserves.

A scalable validation system should classify changes according to their potential impact, establish as much evidence as possible automatically, and route each change to the appropriate level of human judgment.

The goal is not to eliminate code review.

It is to stop treating every change as if it deserves the same kind of review.

The Anatomy of an Evidence Package

Imagine a team where reviewers can safely process about 20 changes per day.

At 20 changes, the system is healthy.

At 35, the backlog grows.

Nothing is necessarily wrong with the developers. The arrival rate of changes has simply exceeded the capacity of the validation system.

Adding more reviewers helps, but it does not scale indefinitely. Senior engineers are expensive, and their attention is often the limiting resource.

The more important question is:

Which changes actually need the same level of human attention?

A scalable review system routes changes according to potential impact, not line count. The pipeline should first establish the change’s potential impact, then determine what evidence is required, and only then decide how much human judgment is necessary.

Instead of this traditional flow: Change → CI → Human Review → Merge

We need a risk-adjusted flow: Change → Risk Classification → Machine Evidence → Validation Tier → Appropriate Human Authority → Merge

Risk is determined by system boundaries. A two-line authorization change requires more scrutiny than a massive formatting update. By pushing tests, contract validation, and dependency analysis as far left as possible, we stop spending engineering attention on information machines can establish reliably.

When an author or agent opens a pull request, the reviewer should not have to manually reconstruct context, trace dependencies, or guess blast radius. The pipeline should construct an initial evidence package before the reviewer begins the review.

An AI-scale Evidence Package answers seven questions:

PULL REQUEST EVIDENCE PACKAGE
│
├── 1. Change       → What changed, and what was intended? (Semantic delta)
├── 2. Impact       → What can this touch? (Blast radius, consumers, call graphs)
├── 3. Risk Tier    → Why did it receive this tier? (Explainable classification)
├── 4. Evidence     → What has been proven deterministically? (Contracts, invariants, tests)
├── 5. Unknowns     → What could NOT be established automatically?
├── 6. Authority    → Who holds the remaining decision rights?
└── 7. Action       → Auto-merge, peer review, domain approval, or escalation

Unknowns may be the most important part of the evidence package.

A mature validation system should not only report what passed. It should explicitly report what it could not establish. An unverified business invariant, an incomplete dependency graph, an ambiguous authorization rule, or an untested failure mode is not an empty field. It is a reason for human attention.

Instead of:

“Here is a 400-line diff. Please find the bugs.”

The pull request becomes:

“Here is what changed, the 5 downstream services it affects, the contract compatibility evidence we gathered, the single invariant we couldn’t prove, and the specific decision required from you.”

The 4-Tier PR Routing Framework

Platform engineering teams must transition from implicit review policies to programmatic enforcement.

The purpose of these tiers is not simply to decide who reviews a pull request. It is to determine what evidence should exist before that review happens.

Classification should happen early, so every pull request enters an appropriate validation path before substantial human review begins.

I recommend four validation tiers:

Tier 0-Deterministic, Low-Risk

These are changes where automation can establish that the potential impact is genuinely constrained.

Examples:

  • Documentation-only changes
  • Comments
  • Controlled configuration
  • Generated artifacts from governed sources
  • Changes that cannot modify executable code or production behavior

Typical checks:

Executable code changed?      No
Security-sensitive path?      No
Public contract changed?      No
Dependency changed?           No
Production configuration?     No
Required checks?              Passed

Action: automated validation → auto-merge where organizational policy permits.

The critical word is deterministically.

A 3-line pull request is not automatically low risk.

A 500-line pull request is not automatically high risk.

The system needs evidence about what the change can affect.

Tier 1-Local Behavior

Imagine adding an endpoint inside an existing service (GET /orders/{order_id}). There are no shared schema changes, no new service dependencies, and existing authentication boundaries remain intact.

The evidence gathered by the pipeline:

Public contract changed?       No
Dependencies changed?          No
Security-sensitive path?       No
Shared schema changed?         No
Tests passed?                  Yes
Affected service count?        1

Action: one peer reviewer.

The reviewer focuses on behavior, design, and intent.

They do not spend most of their time rediscovering information the pipeline has already established.

Tier 2-Shared Contracts and Boundaries

Now consider a seemingly tiny change:

{
  "order_id": "123",
  "customer_id": "456"
}

The change adds one field to an event consumed by five services.

The diff is small.

The blast radius is not.

The evidence gathered by the pipeline:

Contract changed:            OrderCreated
Consumers discovered:        5
Compatibility:               Backward compatible
Contract tests:              5/5 passed
Schema validation:           Passed
Affected services:           5

Action: domain owner review.

Now the senior engineer can answer the question that actually matters: Is this contract change conceptually correct for the business? The pipeline has already established backward compatibility under the relevant checks.

Tier 3-High-Risk Changes

Consider an authorization change:

return user.Role == "admin" &&
       user.TenantID == invoice.TenantID

It is only two lines.

But those two lines modify a security boundary.

That belongs in a fundamentally different validation path.

Typical requirements might include:

Security analysis
        +
Service owner approval
        +
Security owner approval
        +
Relevant integration tests
        +
Staged deployment
        +
Rollback verification
        +
Production monitoring

This is the fundamental principle:

Risk is determined by blast radius and system boundaries, not implementation size.

A two-line authorization change can require more scrutiny than a 500-line UI change.

Make Risk Explainable

Once changes are classified, the next problem is trust.

A developer should never see:

Risk: HIGH
AI confidence: 0.87

and be expected to trust it.

Instead, the system should explain why the change received its tier.

For example:

{
  "tier": 2,
  "reasons": [
    "shared_contract_changed",
    "5_consumers_detected"
  ],
  "evidence": {
    "contract_tests": "5/5",
    "backward_compatible": true,
    "security_paths_changed": false,
    "new_dependencies": false
  }
}

Now the developer can understand the routing decision.

This creates an important distinction:

The system is not claiming that the change is safe.

It is saying:

Here is what we found, here is what we tested, and here is why this change requires this level of validation.

That distinction matters.

Risk classification should be an explainable routing decision, not an opaque AI judgment.

Once pull requests increase, the obvious response is to ask AI to review them.

That is useful.

An AI reviewer can:

  • summarize a change
  • identify suspicious patterns
  • explain unfamiliar code
  • identify missing tests
  • map likely affected components
  • compare implementation against documented requirements
  • suggest areas for human investigation

But there is a critical distinction:

AI-generated code does not become trustworthy simply because another AI reviewed it.

AI can flag that a change modifies authorization behavior, identify affected consumers, or point out missing coverage.

But these outputs are evidence, not authority.

The system should still preserve human authority for decisions where context matters.

The question is therefore not:

Can AI review code?

It clearly can.

The better question is:

Which validation decisions can we automate with sufficient confidence, and which still require human context?

Reviewing Intent, Not Syntax

As automated risk routing clears the PR queue, the nature of human code review must evolve. The most scalable change an engineering team can make is forcing humans to review intent and invariants, rather than spending all their time reading syntax.

Take a payment system where a failed capture can be safely retried, but a retry cannot create a second capture. Those invariants should become executable tests:

Python

def test_capture_is_idempotent():
    first = capture(payment, key="abc")
    second = capture(payment, key="abc")
    assert first.capture_id == second.capture_id

When the machine handles mechanical evidence gathering, the reviewer has a better question to answer: Are these the right invariants? rather than: Did I inspect every one of these 800 AI-generated lines?

Stronger Validation Should Follow Risk

The same principle applies to testing. Traditional test coverage can tell you how much code was executed. It does not necessarily tell you whether the tests would catch a faulty behavior.

Mutation testing provides another signal. For example, if the AI generated:

if (amount <= limit)

A mutation-testing tool will intentionally alter that logic to see if your tests catch it. It might change the code to:

if (amount < limit)

If the test suite still passes, the pipeline has discovered a weakness in the tests. This is especially useful for core business logic, but it should not run exhaustively on every change. Use the same principle as the risk tiers:

  • Tier 0 → Basic deterministic checks
  • Tier 1 → Normal unit/integration tests
  • Tier 2 → Contract testing + deeper behavioral checks
  • Tier 3 → Stronger security, resilience, and mutation testing

The objective is not maximum automation. It is maximum useful evidence for the risk involved.

Make the Pipeline Executable

The architecture becomes truly valuable when it moves from theory into CI/CD.

The routing logic should run early in the pipeline. Here is a simplified GitHub Actions workflow showing how classification can determine which validation stages run:

YAML

name: Pull Request Validation

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  classify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    outputs:
      tier: ${{ steps.risk.outputs.tier }}
      run_contract_tests: ${{ steps.risk.outputs.run_contract_tests }}
      run_security_analysis: ${{ steps.risk.outputs.run_security_analysis }}
      run_mutation_tests: ${{ steps.risk.outputs.run_mutation_tests }}

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Classify change
        id: risk
        shell: bash
        run: |
          ./ci/classify-change.sh \
            --base "${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}" \
            --head "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" \
            > risk.json

          echo "tier=$(jq -r '.tier' risk.json)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "run_contract_tests=$(jq -r '.validation.contract_tests' risk.json)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "run_security_analysis=$(jq -r '.validation.security_analysis' risk.json)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "run_mutation_tests=$(jq -r '.validation.mutation_tests' risk.json)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Publish risk classification
        run: |
          cat risk.json

  validate:
    needs: classify
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run baseline tests
        run: ./ci/test.sh

      - name: Run contract tests
        if: needs.classify.outputs.run_contract_tests == 'true'
        run: ./ci/contract-tests.sh

      - name: Run security analysis
        if: needs.classify.outputs.run_security_analysis == 'true'
        run: ./ci/security-analysis.sh

      - name: Run mutation tests
        if: needs.classify.outputs.run_mutation_tests == 'true'
        run: ./ci/mutation-tests.sh

  report:
    needs: [classify, validate]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Publish evidence package
        run: |
          ./ci/publish-evidence.sh \
            --tier "${{ needs.classify.outputs.tier }}" \
            --status "validated"

A developer looking at this PR should be able to see that it triggered a Tier 2 workflow because it touched a shared contract.

The important property is not the exact script.

It is that the routing decision is inspectable, executable, and transparent.

Measure the Validation System

Once validation becomes a system, it can be measured.

Traditional productivity metrics such as commits, lines of code, pull requests, and story points tell us how much activity is happening.

They do not tell us whether the organization can safely absorb that activity.

Useful measures include:

Arrival rate : how many changes enter validation?

Validation capacity : how many changes can the organization safely process?

Human review time : how much engineering attention does each tier consume?

Auto-validation rate : what percentage of changes can safely proceed without manual intervention?

Escalation rate : how often do changes require higher-level authority?

Classification accuracy : are changes being routed appropriately?

Escaped defects by tier : which classes of changes actually produce production failures?

These measurements create a feedback loop.

If supposedly low-risk changes repeatedly produce incidents, their validation path should become stronger.

If a class of changes accumulates a strong history of safe releases, some manual work may be removable.

The goal is not to automate everything.

It is to continuously improve the relationship between risk, evidence, and human attention.

The New Engineering Constraint

The reviewer no longer needs to discover every piece of information from scratch. The system should bring the relevant evidence to the reviewer. That is the direction in which AI-assisted code review must evolve.

AI has made producing software cheaper.

That does not mean the cost of establishing trust has disappeared.

The wrong response is to ask engineers to review more pull requests.

Another weak response is to put an AI reviewer in front of every pull request and assume the problem is solved.

The better response is to redesign validation around evidence and risk.

  1. Classify the change.
  2. Determine what it can affect.
  3. Gather machine-verifiable evidence.
  4. Apply stronger validation where the risk justifies it.
  5. Route the remaining uncertainty to the right human authority.
  6. The result is not simply a faster code-review process.

It is a different contract between engineers and the software delivery system.

The pull request stops being merely:

“Here is my diff. Please review it.”

And becomes:

“Here is what changed, what it can affect, what we know about it, what we do not know, and the decision that still requires you.”

That is the direction code review needs to take as AI-assisted development becomes the norm.

The scarce resource in a high-velocity engineering organization is no longer the ability to write software.

It is the ability to establish enough evidence to trust, understand, and safely operate the software being produced.

item.title: A Hacker Put His Instagram Ad on Our Website Banner. Our AWS Keys Were Sitting in the Frontend.
item.content:encoded:
Why “it saves backend load” is the wrong reason to expose S3 credentials, and how presigned URLs give you security without any extra load

In my early days as a developer, I joined a project that was already live. A few weeks in, something strange happened. The banner on our website changed.

It wasn’t a design update. It was an advertisement for someone’s Instagram account.

No one on the team had touched it. No deployment went out. The banner had just… changed.

So I started digging.

How the hacker got in

Our app let users upload images directly from the frontend to AWS S3. To make that work, the frontend was using the AWS SDK with an access key and secret key.

Now, the team thought these keys were hidden because they were in environment variables. But here’s the thing many developers miss: anything the frontend uses is public. Environment variables in React, Vue, or any frontend framework get bundled into the JavaScript that ships to the browser.

Open DevTools, check the network requests or the JS bundle, and the keys are right there.

That’s exactly what the hacker did. He found our keys, and since those keys had permission to write to the bucket, he simply uploaded his own image in place of our banner. That was it. No complex exploit, no brute force. We gave him the keys.

And honestly, we were lucky. He only changed a banner. With the same keys, he could have deleted every file in the bucket, or used our S3 to host his own content on our bill.

“But the backend will get more load”

When I asked the team why we weren’t handling uploads through the backend, the answer was:

“If the frontend uploads through our backend, every file passes through our server. That puts more load on the backend. So we upload directly from the frontend. Most startups do it this way.”

And this is a fair concern. If a user uploads a 10 MB file, and it goes frontend → backend → S3, your server has to receive those 10 MB and send them again. Multiply that by thousands of users, and your backend is now a file-transfer server.

But the team was choosing between only two options:

  1. Upload through the backend: secure, but heavy.
  2. Upload from the frontend with AWS keys: light, but completely insecure.

There’s a third option that gives you both.

The fix: presigned URLs

AWS S3 (and almost every object storage service, like Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, or Cloudflare R2) supports presigned URLs.

A presigned URL is a temporary URL that allows exactly one specific action, like “upload one file to this exact path”, for a limited time. The backend creates it using its own credentials, and the frontend uses it to upload directly to S3.

The flow looks like this:

  1. The frontend asks the backend: “I want to upload an avatar image.”
  2. The backend checks whether the user is logged in and allowed to upload.
  3. The backend generates a presigned URL for one specific file path, with a short expiry.
  4. The frontend uploads the file directly to S3 using that URL.
  5. The frontend tells the backend the upload is done.

Now look at what happens to the “backend load” problem. The file never touches your server. The backend only generates a URL, which is a small signing operation done locally with no network call to AWS. The heavy part, the actual file transfer, still goes directly from the browser to S3.

And the AWS keys never leave your backend.

Let’s build it

Here’s the backend part using the AWS SDK v3. I’m using a presigned POST instead of a presigned PUT, because POST lets us enforce rules like
maximum file size, which PUT doesn’t support in the same way.

import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { createPresignedPost } from '@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: 'ap-south-1' });

type UploadRule = {
  maxBytes: number;
  types: string[];
  expiresIn: number;
};

const UPLOAD_RULES: Record<string, UploadRule> = {
  avatar: {
    maxBytes: 2 * 1024 * 1024,
    types: ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'],
    expiresIn: 60,
  },
  document: {
    maxBytes: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
    types: ['application/pdf'],
    expiresIn: 300,
  },
};

export async function createUploadUrl(
  userId: string,
  kind: string,
  contentType: string,
) {
  const rule = UPLOAD_RULES[kind];
  if (!rule) {
    throw new Error('Unknown upload type');
  }
  if (!rule.types.includes(contentType)) {
    throw new Error('File type not allowed');
  }

  // the backend decides the path, not the frontend
  const key = `uploads/${kind}/${userId}/${randomUUID()}`;

  const { url, fields } = await createPresignedPost(s3, {
    Bucket: process.env.UPLOAD_BUCKET!,
    Key: key,
    Conditions: [
      ['content-length-range', 1, rule.maxBytes],
      ['eq', '$Content-Type', contentType],
    ],
    Fields: { 'Content-Type': contentType },
    Expires: rule.expiresIn,
  });

  return { url, fields, key };
}

And the frontend part:

const { url, fields, key } = await api.post('/uploads/url', {
  kind: 'avatar',
  contentType: file.type,
});

const form = new FormData();
Object.entries(fields).forEach(([k, v]) => {
  form.append(k, v as string);
});
form.append('file', file); // the file must be the last field

await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: form });
await api.post('/uploads/confirm', { key });

No AWS keys anywhere in the frontend. The frontend only receives a URL that works for one file, one path, and one minute.

The details that actually make it secure

A presigned URL alone isn’t enough. These details are what would have stopped our hacker.

The backend decides the file path. Notice the key is generated by the backend with a random UUID. The frontend never chooses where the file goes. This is exactly what would have saved our banner: with a presigned URL for uploads/avatar/123/a8f3..., there's no way to overwrite banner.jpg.

Keep the expiry as short as possible. The expiry should depend on the type of upload. A small avatar can upload in seconds, so 60 seconds is plenty. A large document might need a few minutes. The shorter the expiry, the smaller the window for someone to misuse a leaked URL.

Enforce file size and type. The content-length-range condition stops someone from uploading a 5 GB file on your bill. The Content-Type condition makes sure an "image" upload is actually declared as an image.

Only authenticated users get a URL. The endpoint that creates presigned URLs should sit behind your normal auth. Otherwise, anyone can ask for upload URLs.

Give the backend minimal permissions. The IAM role your backend uses should only be allowed to upload to the uploads/ prefix, and nothing else:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:PutObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket/uploads/*"
}

If this role is ever compromised, the damage is still limited.

Configure CORS on the bucket. Since the browser uploads directly to S3, your bucket’s CORS rules must allow POST requests from your domain, and only your domain.

If your keys are already in the frontend

If you’re reading this and realizing your project has the same problem, do this today:

  1. Deactivate and delete the exposed keys in IAM immediately. Removing them from the code isn’t enough, because anyone who already copied them can still use them.
  2. Check CloudTrail for any activity from those keys you don’t recognize.
  3. Switch uploads to presigned URLs as shown above.
  4. Check your bucket for unexpected files, and make sure it doesn’t allow public writes.

Wrapping up

Our team made a trade-off that looked reasonable: security or performance, pick one. But it was a false choice. With presigned URLs, the backend keeps the keys and control, S3 handles the heavy transfer, and the frontend only gets a short-lived permission for one specific file.

A hacker put his Instagram ad on our banner. It was embarrassing, but it was also the cheapest possible way to learn this lesson. It could have been our entire bucket.

So if your frontend has AWS keys in it today, assume someone has already found them.

item.title: Zero-Downtime Updates on a 20M-Row PostgreSQL Table: When to Swap, When to Hash Diff
item.content:encoded:
How we tamed MVCC bloat, lock-queue starvation, and WAL spikes while retroactively mutating 100,000s of historical records.

At our platform, we managed a live 20-million-row PostgreSQL table guarded by multiple composite indexes that required updating hundreds of thousands of historical records every single month.

While append-only inserts (INSERT) are straightforward, attempting large-scale in-place mutations on an active, heavily indexed table immediately surfaced several difficult bottlenecks:

  • Severe MVCC dead tuple accumulation and table bloat as hundreds of thousands of index entries are rewritten
  • Write-Ahead Log (WAL) saturation that drives cloud disk IOPS to their physical ceiling
  • Cascading lock queue contention and 504 Gateway Timeouts that trap short live user read queries behind heavy DML

Operating a non-profit intelligence platform powered by IRS Form 990 tax filings, our team faced a structural challenge: each month’s newly published data required continually updating hundreds of thousands of historical records spanning the prior decade across our 20-million-row database.

To update these 20 million rows safely without causing downtime or query latency spikes for active users, we experimented with and refined a bifurcated approach: Staging Swap vs. Two-Pointer Streaming Hash Diff. Here is what we learned and the operational choices we made along the way.

1. The Core Problem: Continuous Large-Scale Updates on 20 Million Rows

In our non-profit intelligence platform, the core asset is public tax filings from the US Internal Revenue Service: IRS Form 990. Every year, hundreds of thousands of non-profit organizations and private foundations disclose their financials and grant-making activities in these forms.

Our central table, public.grants, contains over 20 million historical grant records. At this volume, spinning up a dedicated Snowflake or ClickHouse cluster represents an unjustified operational tax, yet executing naive full scans or unindexed updates on a single relational instance will instantly paralyze production—an awkward, high-stakes "mid-scale" dataset. To power low-latency multi-dimensional search and analytical dashboards, the table is guarded by key composite indexes:

  • 🔹 Primary Identifier: id (PK)
  • 🔹 Relational Foreign Identifiers: donor_id (funder organization ID), npo_id (grantee organization ID)
  • 🔹 Filtering & Sorting Indexes: grant_year (tax year), grant_amount (dollar amount)
  • 🔹 Composite Relational Indexes: (donor_id, npo_id), (npo_id, donor_id)
💡 Architectural Preconditions: Read-Heavy Dataset & Leaf Table
This operational strategy operates on two critical architectural assumptions:
- Batch-Fed / Read-Heavy Workload: The dataset serves high-concurrency analytical reads with zero live user-facing OLTP writes (e.g., this is not an active e-commerce order or billing ledger subject to concurrent customer writes during execution).
- No Inbound Foreign Keys: The grants table functions as an analytical fact/leaf table. No downstream production tables reference its primary key via inbound foreign key constraints, enabling clean atomic schema swaps without risking relational locking cascades.

The challenge arises during monthly data ingestion. Integrating newly published filings is far from a simple batch INSERT.

Under US tax regulations, non-profit organizations are only required to file comprehensive returns once their annual gross revenue surpasses specific reporting thresholds (typically $50,000+).
Consequently, when emerging non-profits receive grants in their early years, they lack formal public filings. In our database, these historical grants are recorded with raw recipient names (recipient_name), while their foreign entity key (npo_id) remains NULL.

The moment a growing non-profit crosses that revenue threshold and submits its inaugural Form 990, entity resolution matches it to its historical footprint:

[The Monthly Data Pipeline Reality]
Collect new IRS 990 filings ➔ Identify newly registered NPOs (First-time filers)
➔ Match historical records where 'npo_id = NULL' to the newly resolved organization
➔ Triggers massive UPDATE mutations on foreign keys (npo_id) across the existing 20M-row table

Every monthly ingestion batch therefore requires not only inserting new grants, but retroactively updating foreign keys on hundreds of thousands of historical records spanning the prior decade.

Why Naive Batch UPDATEs Fail on Large Indexed Tables

Running standard batch UPDATE statements directly against a live, heavily indexed 20-million-row table triggers three immediate bottlenecks:

  • 🛑 MVCC Dead Tuples & Severe Table Bloat:
    PostgreSQL’s multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) implements an UPDATE by creating a new version of the row and marking the old tuple dead. Updating indexed columns forces new entries into all indexes, rapidly generating gigabytes of dead tuples and blowing up index sizes.
  • 🛑 Write Amplification & WAL Choke:
    Writing hundreds of thousands of random index mutations floods the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), pushing AWS RDS/Aurora disk IOPS to their physical ceiling.
  • 🛑 CPU Spikes & Live Query Starvation:
    Live customer search queries (SELECT * FROM grants WHERE donor_id = ...) get caught behind table locks and disk contention, leading to connection pool exhaustion and cascading 504 Gateway Timeouts.

Our core challenge was straightforward: “Could we complete these massive updates without interrupting user queries or degrading live service availability?”

2. Strategy 1: Staging & Atomic Swap (Blue-Green Replacement)

Our first architecture was an isolated Blue-Green Staging & Swap strategy that leaves the live production table untouched during the heavy lifting.

1) Zero-Impact Bulk Loading and Index Pre-Building

All 20 million records (with the new reconciliations integrated) are written to a completely separate schema: staging.grants.

  • 🔹 Bulk COPY Ingestion: High-throughput tabular streaming directly populates the staging table.
  • 🔹 Pre-Building All Indexes: Composite indexes are built directly on staging.grants. Because the live table (public.grants) is untouched, live user traffic experiences 0% CPU or I/O degradation.
  • 🔹 Pre-Swap Statistical Analysis: Running ANALYZE staging.grants ensures that the PostgreSQL query planner has up-to-date column statistics the microsecond the table goes live.

2) Guarding Connection Pools with Lock Timeouts: SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s'

Once the staging table is populated, indexed, and analyzed, it must swap places with the live table.
Most database textbooks suggest a naive DDL block: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE ... RENAME; COMMIT;.

In a high-throughput 20-million-row production database, running that naive block in production can cause unexpected connection pool exhaustion:

  • 💥 ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Locks and Head-of-Line Blocking:
    ALTER TABLE ... RENAME and ALTER TABLE ... SET SCHEMA require an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock—the strictest lock in PostgreSQL. If a background reporting job or a user dashboard is executing a 10-second SELECT query, the swap transaction must wait in the lock queue.
  • 💥 Cascading Connection Pool Starvation:
    In PostgreSQL, while an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request is queued, every single subsequent query (even a 1ms primary key lookup) is blocked behind it in the queue. Within seconds, all application connection pools are drained, and the entire API fleet begins throwing 504 Gateway Timeouts.

To prevent this, we set an explicit 5-second lock timeout (in ultra-high QPS OLTP, tightening to 1s with retry loops is also effective) and atomically restored all indexes:

BEGIN;
  -- Abort immediately if the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock cannot be acquired within 5s
  SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s';
  -- 1. [CRITICAL] Rename existing live indexes first to free namespace in public schema
  -- (PostgreSQL does NOT automatically rename indexes when a table is renamed; skipping this triggers "relation already exists" collisions)
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.grants_pkey RENAME TO grants_old_pkey;
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.grants_donor_id_idx RENAME TO grants_old_donor_id_idx;
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.grants_npo_id_idx RENAME TO grants_old_npo_id_idx;
  -- ... (Repeat for all remaining composite / filtering indexes)
  -- 2. Rename current live table to _old
  ALTER TABLE IF EXISTS public.grants RENAME TO grants_old;
  -- 3. Promote staging table to public schema
  ALTER TABLE staging.grants SET SCHEMA public;
  -- 4. Restore staging indexes to live production naming conventions
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.staging_grants_pkey RENAME TO grants_pkey;
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.staging_grants_donor_id_idx RENAME TO grants_donor_id_idx;
  ALTER INDEX IF EXISTS public.staging_grants_npo_id_idx RENAME TO grants_npo_id_idx;
  -- ... (Repeat for all remaining staging indexes)
COMMIT;
💡 Why Fail-Fast with a Lock Timeout?
If the lock cannot be acquired within 5 seconds, PostgreSQL terminates the DDL with ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout and immediately rolls back.
The batch job fails temporarily, but the hundreds of incoming user queries waiting behind it are immediately released to complete normally. Protecting live customer queries was far more critical; by aborting early, we could safely retry the swap when traffic quieted down.

Following a successful swap, the previous table (grants_old) was retained for a defined "bake period" (several hours) rather than dropped immediately. This provided an instant, zero-downtime rollback safety net—allowing a 50ms reverse swap if data anomalies or application regressions were uncovered. Once health metrics stabilized, the table was asynchronously dropped outside the transaction (DROP TABLE IF EXISTS public.grants_old;).

⚠️ Two Critical Production Operational Caveats
- Temporary Disk Headroom (2x Storage Watermark): Holding a staging table alongside index sort temp files (pgsql_tmp) requires temporary disk headroom of at least 2x during the build and swap phases.
- Foreign Keys & Dependent Views: grants was an independent leaf table with zero inbound foreign key constraints or dependent database views, allowing clean swapping. Tables with inbound dependencies require separate FK migration routines.

3. Strategy 2: Two-Pointer Streaming Hash Diff (0.5% Incremental Ingestion)

While Staging & Swap provided rock-solid reliability, operational overhead emerged as the dataset scaled.

Each month, new IRS filings only modified or added approximately 100,000 rows — merely 0.5% of the total 20 million rows.

“Does it make sense to copy 20 million rows and rebuild massive indexes every month just to update 0.5% of the data?”

Full rebuilds consumed excessive batch compute time and generated massive, unnecessary disk write churn. To optimize this, we built a Two-Pointer Streaming Hash Diff pipeline that surgically isolates modified rows with constant O(1) memory.

1) Generator-Based Keyset Hash Streaming

In reality, each grant record contained extensive textual metadata — such as multi-paragraph grant descriptions (grant_description), grantee mission statements, and over ten auxiliary metadata fields. Streaming all 20 million full-width records over the network every month would have wasted 10GB to 20GB of network bandwidth and saturated worker memory.

Instead of transmitting bulky text or executing heavy database-side joins/EXCEPT queries, our keyset cursor projected only two lightweight columns—the identifier (id) and a 32-character MD5 hash (roughly 40 bytes per row)—streamed in chunks of 100,000:

SELECT id, MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', COALESCE(donor_id::text, ''), COALESCE(npo_id::text, ''), ...))
FROM public.grants
WHERE id > %s
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100000;
  • 🔹 Over 90% Network Egress Reduction: Even when scanning all 20 million records, transmitting only primary keys and 32-character hashes condensed an otherwise massive multi-gigabyte payload down to approximately 800MB.
  • 🔹 Cursor-Based Keyset Pagination (WHERE id > %s): OFFSET pagination re-reads and discards all preceding rows on every batch, causing individual query latency to degrade linearly (O(K) where K is the offset row count) and cumulative disk scans across the full table to explode quadratically (O(N²)). In contrast, index-seek keyset cursors jump directly to the target leaf page via B-Tree seek, keeping individual batch query times uniformly fast (~0.1s) and bounding cumulative full-table traversal to a predictable linear cost (O(N)).
  • 🔹 Live DB CPU Conservation: The database performs lightweight index seeks and compact hash projections, offloading 100% of the row-by-row diff comparison to external worker processes.

2) Two-Pointer Sorted Merge Diff for O(1) Memory

Loading 20 million live hashes into a Python dictionary would consume gigabytes of memory.
However, because both incoming source records and the live database keyset cursor are ordered by id, an in-memory hash map is completely unnecessary.

Advancing cursors across both streams simultaneously via a Two-Pointer Linear Merge (O(N)) retains only the active batch buffer in memory, keeping worker memory flat under 50MB (O(1) memory) regardless of table size:

  • 🔹 Key Match & Hash Mismatch: Classified as mutated row (to_upsert); advance both pointers
  • 🔹 Source Key < Live Key: Classified as new insertion (to_upsert); advance source pointer
  • 🔹 Source Key > Live Key: Classified as deletion; advance live pointer
  • 🔹 Deletion Handling: Because non-profit tax filings are cumulative disclosures where grants are additive or amended rather than deleted, real-world deletions were virtually 0%, allowing the pipeline to concentrate on to_upsert.

In a single linear pass over 20 million records, this algorithm isolates the exact 100,000 modified records (to_upsert) in minutes with near-zero memory footprint.

3) UNLOGGED Temporary Tables and B-Tree Space Reuse

The 100,000 identified rows are written via high-speed COPY into an UNLOGGED temporary table (grants_upsert_tmp). Utilizing an UNLOGGED table completely eliminates Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) for the intermediate buffer, halving write I/O.

We then merge them into the live table in a set-based operation using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE:

INSERT INTO public.grants (id, donor_id, npo_id, grant_year, grant_amount, recipient_name)
SELECT id, donor_id, npo_id, grant_year, grant_amount, recipient_name
FROM public.grants_upsert_tmp
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET
  grant_year = EXCLUDED.grant_year,
  npo_id = EXCLUDED.npo_id,
  donor_id = EXCLUDED.donor_id,
  grant_amount = EXCLUDED.grant_amount,
  recipient_name = EXCLUDED.recipient_name;
  • 🔹 Guaranteed Idempotency: If subtle serialization formatting differences between Python and PostgreSQL casting occasionally flag an unmutated row as changed, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE executes idempotently with zero risk to data integrity.
  • 🔹 B-Tree Space Reuse Over Redundant REINDEX (VACUUM ANALYZE):
    Mutating indexed foreign keys (npo_id) forces Non-HOT updates, generating new index tuples. However, updating 100,000 rows (0.5%) creates less than 1% fragmentation across B-Tree leaf pages. Triggering REINDEX CONCURRENTLY across all 20 million rows would waste 20+ GB of WAL and burn 40 minutes of disk I/O, defeating the purpose of an incremental diff.
    PostgreSQL 14+'s B-Tree Bottom-Up Index Deletion and LP_DEAD tuple pruning proactively clean up dead index pointers right before page splits occur, while the Heap Free Space Map (FSM) recycles dead tuple slots.
    Crucially, PostgreSQL’s default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is 0.2 (20%), meaning on a 20M-row table, autovacuum will not trigger until at least 4 million dead tuples accumulate. A 0.5% (100k) delta will be completely ignored by the background autovacuum daemon. Explicitly executing VACUUM ANALYZE immediately following the batch run is mandatory to bulk-prune dead index pointers and refresh optimizer statistics, without ever resorting to a heavy full REINDEX.

4. Architectural Retrospective: Static Datastores and Conscious Technical Debt

The defining characteristic of this dataset is that it is a 100% static, read-only database to live users — there are zero user-driven writes during production.

Objectively speaking, for a static dataset with no live user mutations, there was never a strict, fundamental requirement to keep it confined within the same relational database serving core user authentication and transaction workloads.

Before reaching for exotic new technologies, the most natural first-step architecture would be to keep PostgreSQL, but physically isolate the 20-million-row static dataset (grants) into its own dedicated database instance and perform application-level joins. This offers immediate advantages:

  • It completely eliminates I/O competition and DDL lock interference with live service tables (user accounts, bookmarks, billing).
  • It preserves 100% of the engineering team’s existing PostgreSQL operational playbooks and tooling with zero learning curve.

However, given the operational realities and limited engineering bandwidth of a lean startup team, provisioning another dedicated database instance and maintaining cross-database application join logic still represented a substantial operational tax (Ops Tax).

Furthermore, because our business API logic still required relational joins across non-profit entities, adopting dedicated columnar engines like ClickHouse or embedded stores like DuckDB was postponed for a future architectural milestone. We ultimately chose a deliberate compromise:

  • 🔹 Maintaining a Single Datastore: We chose to stick with our existing single PostgreSQL instance, leveraging Keyset pagination, UNLOGGED temp tables, and lock timeouts to meet our performance needs.
  • 🔹 Conscious Technical Debt: We accepted co-locating this large static dataset in our primary relational database as an explicit, well-contained “Conscious Technical Debt.”
💡 Why Not Native Declarative Partitioning?
Partitioning by tax year (grant_year) seems appealing for partition swapping (ATTACH/DETACH PARTITION). However, over 80% of our real-world user queries aggregate a funder's complete 10-year multi-year trajectory or perform cross-year analyses. Partitioning would force the query planner to scan multiple sub-table index trees, increasing planning overhead. Maintaining a monolithic table ensured maximum index efficiency and full backward compatibility with existing API endpoints.

At our current 20-million-row scale, this setup delivers stable sub-second production performance and 100% uptime. As our dataset inevitably expands toward 50M to 100M+ rows, our roadmap will pay down this technical debt in phases: first by isolating dedicated PostgreSQL instances with application-level joins, and subsequently by adopting DuckDB embedded caching or ClickHouse analytical clusters.

5. When to Swap vs. When to Diff

After running both approaches in production, we settled on a simple rule of thumb for when to use each:

  • ⚡ Hash Diff Upsert Strategy (Monthly Incremental Ingestion)
    ➔ Trigger: Monthly retroactive updates driven by newly filed IRS 990s (~100K rows, ~0.5% delta)
    ➔ Pros: Eliminates 20M-row index rebuilds, zero intermediate WAL via UNLOGGED staging, automatic B-tree page space reuse via VACUUM ANALYZE
    ➔ Operational Perk: Even if minor serialization quirks between Python and PostgreSQL casting cause an unchanged row to be rewritten, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE operates idempotently with zero data integrity risk.
  • 🔄 Staging & Swap Strategy (Schema Migrations / Annual Baseline Reconciliation)
    ➔ Trigger: Table schema DDL alterations (adding/modifying columns), major index redesigns, or annual full-table integrity reconciliations
    ➔ Pros: Purges 100% of dead tuples and index bloat, executes in <50ms atomic swap protected by lock_timeout = '5s', provides instant rollback safety via retained previous table
    ➔ Caution: Requires temporary disk headroom of at least 2x to accommodate the staging table and index sort temp files

6. Wrapping Up: Practical Lessons Learned

  • 🎯 Explore Your Existing Stack Before Adding New Tools:
    When managing static datasets, it is tempting to jump straight to specialized OLAP or embedded columnar engines. For a small team, however, the extra operational tax often outweighs the benefits. While running static data in PostgreSQL may not be textbook perfection, making good use of its native mechanics (Keyset cursor streaming, UNLOGGED tables, B-Tree space reuse) allowed us to reliably serve 20 million rows without expanding our infrastructure complexity.
  • 🎯 Breaking the Lock Queue Is the Real Secret to Safe DDL:
    The biggest risk in a large table swap is rarely the DDL execution time itself, but Head-of-Line Blocking — where fast, innocent user read queries pile up behind a waiting DDL lock. Using SET LOCAL lock_timeout to quickly fail fast and back off was the single most effective safeguard for keeping our live service responsive.
  • 🎯 Bifurcate Updates by Operational Goal:
    For routine monthly updates where only ~0.5% of records mutate, Two-Pointer Hash Diffing with VACUUM ANALYZE provides a lightweight, idempotent path. For structural schema DDL migrations or full baseline resets, Staging & Swap delivers a pristine, bloat-free foundation—giving us the best of both worlds.
